- One commitment per line.
- Write each as a verb phrase: an action followed by its object. For example: "raise the income tax threshold" or "build 300000 new homes".
- State each commitment at the level of a distinct policy action, not its implementation details. Do not subdivide a single commitment into steps.
- Include every commitment. Do not select, rank, prioritise, or judge importance.
- Use the text's own terms for policy objects. Do not substitute synonyms.

# Summary of the 2005 Manifesto

This manifesto presents a comprehensive policy platform organised around ten main areas, emphasising sustainability, social equity, and democratic reform.

## Economic Policy

The document advocates for wealth redistribution through restructured taxation, including additional income tax bands for higher earners and reformed corporation tax with more bands for larger companies. It proposes replacing VAT with environmental taxes based on resource usage, pollution, and waste. A Land Value Tax would replace council tax and business rates. The manifesto promotes economic localisation through community banks, credit unions, and local currencies, while opposing the single European currency. It suggests replacing GDP with alternative measures of wellbeing such as the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare.

## Energy and Climate

The manifesto adopts "Contraction and Convergence" principles, targeting 20% carbon dioxide reduction by 2010, 50% by 2020, and 85% by 2030. It proposes a carbon tax based on fuel carbon content, increasing renewable energy to 40% by 2020, and closing nuclear power stations as they reach end-of-life. Domestic energy demand would be reduced by 30% within ten years through improved building standards.

## Welfare Reform

Central to welfare policy is a Citizen's Income—an unconditional, non-means-tested payment for all residents covering basic needs, alongside a Citizen's Pension guaranteeing retirement income linked to average earnings. Working hours would be reduced through enforcement of the 48-hour working week limit, with potential further reduction to 35 hours.

## Health and Education

The manifesto commits to restoring public health services to founding principles, opposing private sector involvement and commercialisation. It proposes abolishing prescription charges, reintroducing free eye tests and dental care, and increasing health funding to 9% of national income. Education reforms include abolishing tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, and replacing standardised testing with individualised learning plans.

## Transport

Transport policy prioritises sustainable modes over private vehicles, targeting 10% road traffic reduction by 2010. Public transport would be improved and made cheaper than driving, with rail and underground networks returned to public ownership. Environmental costs of motoring would be incorporated into pricing, and aviation fuel taxation would be introduced.

## Environment

A Zero Waste Strategy would eliminate incineration, mandate recycled content standards, and target 60% domestic waste recycling by 2010. An Environmental Protection Commission would coordinate research on public health and environmental protection. The document opposes genetic modification, supports animal welfare legislation, and advocates ending patents on natural genetic resources.

## Food and Agriculture

The manifesto targets 30% organic food production by 2012, proposing to replace existing agricultural and fisheries policies with support for local food production and smaller farms. It advocates banning genetically modified food and strengthening regulations on supermarket practices.

## Crime and Justice

Crime reduction focuses on community-based prevention, addressing social causes, improving urban design, and expanding youth facilities. Community policing would be increased, with police more accountable to local government. Restorative justice programmes would be expanded. Stricter gun control legislation would define lethal weapons quantitatively and create unified licensing.

## Democratic Reform

Constitutional reforms include introducing proportional representation for elections, creating an elected upper legislative chamber, establishing a written constitution, and opposing national identity cards. Local government would receive enhanced powers including local taxation authority. Regional government would be democratised.

## International Policy

Foreign policy emphasises diplomacy, arms reduction, and nuclear disarmament. Military spending would decrease to European averages. Overseas aid would increase to 1% of national income, with debt cancellation for the poorest countries. The document advocates reforming international trade rules to permit discrimination favouring local production, environmental protection, and human rights, while opposing the proposed European constitutional treaty as insufficiently democratic.
